t: 2846. Minimum Edge Weight Equilibrium Queries in a Tree
o: For each query (a,b), find the path's edge count and the most frequent weight on it; the answer is pathLength − maxFrequency (change all edges to the modal weight). Weights are only 1..26, so we can store, for every ancestor jump of length 2^k, a 26-length count vector of edge weights covered — enabling O(26·log n) path queries via binary lifting LCA. Example 1, query (0,6): path has 3 edges of weight 1 and 3 of weight 2 → 6 − 3 = 3. With n ≤ 1e4 and m ≤ 2e4, this fits comfortably; per-query BFS would be O(m·n) ≈ 2e8, borderline but included as a simpler baseline.
k: Answer = path edge count − max frequency of any weight on the path.
Binary lifting with 26-value count vectors merges counts along jumps in O(26) per level.
Root the tree, store depth, 2^k ancestors, and cumulative weight counts per jump.

a.n: Approach 1: Brute Force Path Walk per Query
a.i: For each query, walk from a and b upward to the root recording edges, find the intersection point, tally the 26 weights on the path, and subtract the max tally from the path length. Simple and correct; relies on small limits.
s: Per query, collect (ancestor, weight) chains from a and b to root; locate the deepest common node.
Count weights along a→LCA and b→LCA; answer = totalEdges − maxCount.
a.t: O(m·n) worst case — each query walks up to O(n) ancestors (≈2e8 simple ops, usually fast in practice due to shallow trees)

a.n: Approach 2: Binary Lifting with Weight Counts
a.i: Precompute up[k][v] (2^k-th ancestor) and cnt[k][v][26] (weight counts of the 2^k edges above v). Lift the deeper node, then lift both jointly; merge 26-vectors per jump. Each query costs O(26 log n).
s: Root at 0; BFS to set depth, parent, and cnt[level 0] (copy parent's counts, add the connecting edge's weight).
Build levels k = 1..LOG merging child and parent-of-parent count vectors.
Per query: equalize depths by lifting (accumulating counts), then descend jointly while ancestors differ; finally add the two level-0 counts.
a.t: O((n + m) · 26 · log n) — table build is n·log n·26; each query merges O(log n) vectors of size 26
a.sp: O(n · log n · 26) — the lifting count tables

w: Present the brute-force walk first (it's often accepted here), then binary lifting as the robust solution. Memory is the main concern for lifting: n·14·26 ints ≈ 3.6M entries — fine. Pitfalls: converting weights to 0-indexed consistently, handling a == b after depth equalization (skip the joint descent), and remembering the final level-0 additions cover the last edges to the LCA. Follow-up: dynamic edge updates would require Heavy-Light decomposition with segment trees.
